Maladaptive Strategies.value: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed
I am permanently an outsider now

vignette:
Nadia is a 68-year-old prison guard who has worked in a maximum-security facility for over thirty years. She is married, with adult children who live out of state. The event that changed everything happened eighteen months ago, during a routine cell block count. A group of inmates orchestrated a coordinated assault. Nadia was knocked to the ground, and as she tried to radio for backup, she watched two younger officers get dragged into a corner and beaten before help arrived. She was rescued before she could be seriously injured, but the image of those officers falling—and the sound of the sudden, unnatural quiet that preceded the attack—stayed with her.

In the weeks that followed, Nadia found she could not bear to be alone with her thoughts. She began filling every waking hour with company: calling her sister for hours, visiting neighbors, lingering in the break room long after her shift ended. At home, she would keep the television on all night, talk to her husband until he fell asleep, and then lie awake staring at the ceiling. Sleep came only in fragments, always interrupted by the sensation of the cold floor against her cheek. She would startle at the slightest creak of the house. Silence itself became a threat: if the television paused or her husband stopped breathing in his sleep, her heart would race, her hands would tremble, and she would be on her feet before her mind understood why. Her body reacted to danger before she had time to think, and she had come to believe that her instincts had failed her that day—that she should have seen it coming, should have protected her colleagues. The thought burned: *I failed. I am no longer one of them.*

She began to drop responsibilities. She stopped volunteering for overtime, then stopped attending staff meetings, then stopped driving her husband to his appointments because the route passed the road leading to the prison. She avoided the grocery store at certain hours. She gave up her role as a mentor to new officers because she could not bear to stand in the same hallway where the assault occurred. Her supervisor noticed her absences, her reduced availability; Nadia made excuses about her age, about retirement planning. But inside, she felt an unshakable distance from everyone. She had become an outsider among people she had worked beside for decades. She found herself scanning every room she entered—the prison cafeteria, her own kitchen—checking exits, watching hands, noting where people were standing. She mistrusted even those she had known for years. When a colleague smiled at her, she wondered what they were hiding.

At home, her husband grew frustrated. He would find her standing at the living room window at 2 a.m., staring at the streetlamp. When he asked what was wrong, she would say, “Nothing,” but she could not stop checking the shadows. She had started sleeping in separate rooms so her restlessness would not wake him. She felt guilty—she knew she was pushing him away—but she could not explain why every silence felt like the moment before the attack. She had stopped calling her children because she had nothing to say that wasn’t about safety, about threat, about the feeling that the world was about to collapse.

What finally brought Nadia to seek help was a minor incident: she nearly hit a pedestrian because she had been checking the rearview mirror for a car that might be following her. Her husband insisted she see someone. She came to therapy not because she believed talking would help, but because she was exhausted. She feared she would never feel safe again, and she was terrified that she had already lost the person she used to be—the guard who had been steady, trusted, and capable. She hoped, without much conviction, that she might find a way to sleep through a single night.
